div.p: In the presentation, the most important and necessary properties of embedded real-time systems, and the ways to achieve them, will be explored. The basic and most important domains of real-time systems design will be dealt with, starting with the processor and system hardware architectures, over operating systems, tasking and scheduling, high-level real-time programming languages, worst case execution time and schedulability analysis, to application design engineering and safety critical applications. Common misconceptions which are still strongly present in the control systems design will be identified, guidelines for the consistent implementation will be proposed and sample solutions in certain areas will be presented.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Mechatronic approach in the modern design of complex products is getting more and more attention lately. Mechatronic systems ( "systems for perception and action") consist of three main physical components. mechanic, electrical and computer subsystems. The latter are often called embedded computer control systems. By definition they operate in hard real-time domain: they must be permanently ready to respond to the requests from the environment in the pre-determined time frames; hence their other names, responsive or reactive systems.

Some twenty years ago the discipline of real-time systems began to gain increasingly more and more interest. All domains involved got a lot attention from computer scientists all over the world and from most major domains of computer science. Ultimate guidelines for their design have changed from fast to fast enough: it is of utmost importance that the systems meet their pre-set deadlines. To be able to achieve that, determinism and predictability of temporal behaviour of tasks' program execution is necessary: these properties essentially imply other requirements. , Unfortunately, although there is no dispute on that among scientists. the state-of-the-art in practical applications is still far from meeting (or even proving) these requirements: in general, program execution and system response times are usually unpredictable and not consistently analysed. Hence, the state-of-the-art in performance verification of control systems is

div.head: Hope and Pray!
div.p: The reason for that is that common hardware and software means which are employed in control applications are optimised for their average performance, whereas to guarantee meeting the deadlines it is nec-0-7803-5662-4/99/$10.00 01999 IEEE essary to consider worst-case behaviour. In the execution time analysis there is certain amount of pessimism necessarily involved, diminishing the estimated average performance considerably.

To avoid having to use more powerful hardware platforms because of these pessimistic estimations designers tend to develop and test the control application in usual way, risking that the deadlines will be missed; the consequences, however, could be severe in certain cases, like massive material loss or even endangerment of human safety. This is a situation that soon must be overcame; the gap between the academic research results and the practical implementation must be abolished in order to provide for much more consistent and safer computer control systems.

In the paper, first the basic properties of real-time systems will be briefly mentioned. Then, some domains explicitly involved in embedded systems design will be dealt with, like hardware architectures, operating system issues, languages, compilers, worst case execution time analysis, etc. A special section is dedicated to safety-critical systems, bearing in mind that most control systems are to certain extent safety-critical. Although interesting and relevant to some more sophisticated computer control systems, higher-level issues like more advanced software engineering topics, real-time data bases or artificial intelligence will not be dealt with here.

div.head: REAL-TIME SYSTEMS
div.p: Real-time operation is operating mode of a computer system in which programs for processing of data arriving from outside are permanently ready, so that their results will be available within predetermined periods of time. The arrival times of the data can be randomly distributed or be already a priori determined depending on different applications [3]. Although functionally correct, results produced beyond the pre-determined time frames are wrong.

In computer control systems it is distinguished between hard-and soft real-time requirements. Whereas in a case of soft real-time the penalty when missing a deadline increases with time, in the hard real-time the results are useless with any consequences that may bring. General optimisation criterium in soft real-time matters is average performance while in hard real-time environments it is necessary to consider the worst case behaviour. Most of the systems, however, are hybrid: hard and soft real-time tasks usually co-exist in applica-tions, where hard real-time tasks as a rule execute with higher priority, and the soft real-time ones run within their performance reserve.
There are two different comprehensions of the predictability: layer-by-layer (microscopic) and top-layer (macroscopic) predictability [13].

Layer-by layer predictability requires each of the layers in the real-time application design to behave deterministically and predictably, thus providing the necessary basis for the next layer. This approach is suitable for embedded control systems with moderate complexity; it was shown that their temporal behaviour can be a-priori guaranteed [6].

Top-layer predictability only considers the behaviour on the highest (application) layer and provides handlers to deal with missing the deadlines; this concept is suitable for sophysticated and complex applications where it is impossible to deal with time in detail. However, in embedded systems, especially those with high integrity requirements for safety critical applications, it is necessary to strive for microscopic predictability.

Beside timeliness and Predictability, an important property of control systems is dependability. Hardware part of these systems has already reached a high degree of dependability; methods and techniques for their verification has been well established.

Dependability of the software is still far behind. The reason for that is its inherent complexity. Unfortunately, software engineering has not made a lot of progress in this specific field, yet. For the time being, the most important principle to be followed, when designing a system with severe dependability requirements, is simplicity.

Simple solutions, however, are the most difficult ones: they require high innovation and complete intellectual penetration of issues: Progress is the road from the primitive via the complicated to the simple.
Easy understandability is the most important precondition to prove the correctness of a system.

div.head: HARDWARE ARCHITECTURES
div.p: In common state-of-the-art control computers, usually conventional microprocessors are used, which are optimised for best utilisation in the average case. This, however, is in contradiction with the hard real-time optimisation criterium, the worst-case performance.

Processor utilisation itself is category of 1960's and 1970's and is now obsolete due to the achievements in solid-state technology and, consequently, the availability and prices of hardware components. Sub-optimal utilisation is a cheap price to be paid for simplicity and dependability.

div.head: A . Undesirable properties of conventional architectures
div.p: Undesirable properties of conventional architectures are those which make system's temporal behaviour (1) unpredictable or/and (2) difficult for estimation. A common counterproductive charact,eristic of their design is excessive complexity, which makes their verification difficult or impossible.

The increase in microprocessor performance through the years was mainly influenced by two factors, viz., technological advances and new ideas employed in architectural design. These new ideas are, e.g., the RISC philosophy, parallel processing (pipelining), caching, and others. While RISC ideas are very suitable also for architectures employed in hard real-time systems because of their simplicity and verifiability achieved, the other two features (although always present also in RISC processors) present a hazard to determinism and predictability of their temporal behaviour.

div.head: Independent parallel operation of internal components.
div.p: In order to fully exploit inherent parallelism of operations, the internal units of processors were becoming more and more autonomous resulting in highly asynchronous operation. By this development the average performance of processors is increased. However, it is a complex task to analyse corresponding sequences of machine code instructions in order to determine their execution times. For the time being, verification of such complex processors is practically impossible.

The most common way of improving the throughput of a processor by exploiting instruction level parallelism is pipelining. Various techniques are used to cope with the well-known pipeline breaking problem due to the dependence of instruction flow control on the results generated by previous instructions, but are all based on optimisation of the average performance.

To predict execution times, complex machine code analysers would be necessary, based on detailed information about instruction execution, which is often proprietary and thus inaccessible. Owing to its complexity, a processor with pipelined operation is also very difficult to verify.

Caching. Fetching data from off-processor sources represents a traditional bottle-neck, especially in the von Neumann processor concept. To avoid it, cache memories were introduced. Since instruction fetching from memory takes a considerable amount of execution time, the latter thus highly depends on whether an instruction was found in the cache or not. To predict that, complex analysers would be necessary, emulating the caching operation. Even the most sophisticated ones would fail in the case of multiprogramming, where caches are filled with new contents on every context switch.

Similar to processor architecture considerations, in classical system architecture design some features were implemented to improve average performance. Again, these features may lead to undesirable consequences which make process execution time prediction difficult or even impossible. Some of them are listed in the sequel. Direct memory access. With respect to the delays caused by DMA transfers, there are two general modes of DMA operation, viz., the cycle stealing and the burst mode. A DMA controller operating in the cycle stealing mode is literally stealing bus cycles from the processor, while in the other mode the processor is stopped until the DMA transfer is completed. Although the processor has no control over its system during such a delay, this mode is more appropriate when predictability is the main issue. If block length and data transfer initiation instant are known at compile time, the delay can be calculated and considered in the program execution time estimation. Furthermore, block transfer is also faster, because bus arbitration needs only to be done once.

Data transfer protocols. Data transfer via microcomputer busses also deserves some consideration. Synchronous data transfer protocols by definition ensure predictable data transfer times. Asynchronous ones are more flexible, however, their behaviour is very difficult to control, especially in shared-bus systems. The best way to guarantee realistic data transfer times seems to be synchronous operation of all potential bus masters.

Similar conclusions hold for local area networks as well. For distributed control systems appropriate network protocols with deterministic and predictable behaviour must be chosen. Widely used CSMA/CD (Ethernet) is inapropriate because of non-deterministic resolution opf colisions. A frequent problem is also complexity of standard protocols: the standard document DIN 19245 on fieldbus Profibus has 750 pages.

Exception and interrupt handling. The problems discussed in previous paragraphs could either be prevented or the measures potentially causing nondeterministic or unpredictable behaviour could be renounced. However, in process control computers operating in dynamic mode, i.e. immediately responding to the events in their environments, exceptions and especially interrupts are inavoidable. Since these events happen asynchronously to the program executions, the program execution is necessarly delayed. The problem can not be solved in classical single processor architectures.

The solution to this problem is to employ a dedicated asymmetrical multiprocessor architecture in which one processor is handling such events as signals from the environment, time events, changes of synchronisers. etc. , and performing functions of the operating system kernel.

When such an event occurs, the corresponding task is put into a ready state and re-scheduling is done; all that is happening in parallel with the execution of the running task without interrupting it. Knowing the (residual) execution times of application programs the runtime schedulability analyser checks whether there exists a feasible schedule of the new set of tasks. If it does, the tasks are re-scheduled accordingly.

Apart of provision for predictability, also the inherent parallelism of task execution and operating system administration routines is exploited thus considerably improving systems performance. Also, the counterproductive overhead of context switching is minimised.
This solution have been implemented in several academic prototype platforms [l], [12], [2], while no reports have been found on actual industrial implementations.

div.head: IV. OPERATING SYSTEMS, TASKING AND SCHEDULING
div.p: According to the nature, scale, purpose, implementation, etc., in embedded real-time control systems different options can be found considering the system software functions. In some larger scale and complex control applications complete operating systems can be observedIn smaller applications only real-time executives are sufficient, providing basic functions like task and time management, interrupt and error handling, etc. Often, these functions are custom designed and included into the integral application program code.
Common functions of the real-time operating systems for embedded applications are [15]:
interrupt handling: lowest level routines, direct hardware support;
process management: multiprogramming is supported by the concept of processes and tasks, which are supervised by process and task management;

inter-process communication and synchronisation: means for interaction between asynchronously operating processes and tasks; time management: administration of time, actions on processes and tasks on specified instants of time;

inputoutput drivers: support for communication with peripheral devices; man-machine communication: support for the interaction between the system and the operator: file management: not obligatory in embedded systems; memory management: storage administration supports robustness and safety of control systems. Virtual memory is jeopardising predictability considering the variable access times of data residing in the memory or on mass storage medium; it is obsolete due to the very large semiconductor memories available;

error handling: necessary for robust fault tolerant systems. Its implementation must allow for the consideration of delays in error situations; exception handling: one of the most severe obstacles to predictability of execution times of tasks; a good solution is to handle exceptions off-line, in parallel on a dedicated processor (see above).

Application programs controlling the processes are organised in tasks. Tasks embody application programs whose worst case execution times are analysed and thus known. Important parameter of each task is its deadline, usually expressed as an interval from the tasks's invocation until the instant when it needs to be concluded. If it is not, the deadline is violated with the consequences which depend on whether the task is a hard or a soft one. In the former case the task has failed, the results are meaningless and the system is in a fault condition.

Computer control systems can be of either static or dynamic nature. The operation of the static systems is controlled synchronously by programs, i.e. it can be prepared in advance. There are no interrupts or other events. Scheduling of tasks is done at the design time; it can be analysed, tested and verified a priori.
Such systems are much safer and more robust than the dynamic ones.

However, in most cases it is not possible to assume the behaviour of the system in advance. In these cases it is necessary to consider dynamic events at the run time. Verification of such systems is much more demanding.

In dynamic multi-tasking systems, adequate scheduling algorithms to generate appropriate schedules must be implemented. The ones which guarrantee to fulfil the requirement that all tasks must meet their deadlines (provided the system's performance is sufficient) are referred to as feasible. In the literature, several such algorithms have been reported. Actually, scheduling of real-time tasks is a very popular research area although most adequate basic policies have been known since quite a long time.

The usual means to introduce asynchronous dynamic events to the microproceesor based control systems are interrupts. Handling of them by the microprocessors is as a rule priority based, and this policy can usually be found in real-time executives. However, it is not, possible to guarrantee schedulability [14] of a set of ready tasks by assigning them static priorities; although this technique is temp\ing simple and broadly used, it is highly inappropriate for hard real-time applications.

In dynamic system tasks can be activated 'periodically or sporadically; a suitable scheduling policy for periodic tasks is rate-monotonic scheduling [9]: the task with the highest frequency of invocations is assigned highest dynamic priority.

For sporadic task activations, one of the most suitable seems to be the earliest-deadline-first scheduling algorithm: the task with the closest deadline is executed first (a modified version is described in [l]). It has been shown that it is feasible for scheduling tasks on single processor systems; with the throw-forward extension it is also feasible on homogeneous multiprocessor systems. However, this extension leads to more preemptions and is more complex and, thus, less practical.

For process control applications, where process interfaces are usually physically hard-wired to sensors and actuators establishing the contact to the environment, it is natural to implement either single processor systems or dedicated multiprocessors. Thus, the earliestdeadline-first scheduling policy can be employed without causing any restrictions, resulting in a number of advantages [6].

div.head: V. PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES AND WORST CASE EXECUTION T I M E AN ALY S IS
div.p: In process control two categories of control computers are generally used: generic computer systems and industrial programmable controllers. For programming the former, universal high level programming languages are used; unfortunately, a considerable part of applications is stil programmed in assembly language what means much more error-prone programs and less productive application program development. Industrial controllers are programmed using a variety of vendor specific programming means.

div.head: A . High-level real-tame programming languages
div.p: A high-level programming language to be implemented in a real-time environment should fulfill the following properties: support for predictability of temporal behaviour of programs: most of the commercially available and broadly used languages do not fully meet that requirement. It is thus left to the programmer to use for the sensible parts of the application only the constructs which do not jeopardise the predictability, and to analyse and at the run-time supervise the temporal behaviour of the programi it should be secure to allow for reliability of programs: it should support strong type checking and make provision for exception handling;

support for multiprogramming: it should include task support and good synchronisation means; it should provide good hardware access: peripheral device drivers are a very common and important part of real-time applications;
support for programming-in-the-large: it should be modular and allow separate compilation;
it should be well maintainable: real-time software has a long life expectancy; programs should be easy to read, understand, and modify.
High-level programming languages for programming generic computer systems used in control applications can be further divided into two categories: implementation languages and real-time languages.

Implementation languages do not provide much support for real-time programming. Application programmer has to call certain library or operating system kernel routines which deal with the real-time requirements to certain extent. Among implementation languages by far the most common is C or C++. Its advantages are good availability, connectivity with, and support for, program development tools; most programmers are familiar with it; the disadvantage is poor readability and maintainability, and the lack of almost any of the above requirements for real-time programming.

For programming real-time applications, proper realtime programming languages should be used. There are not many such languages commercially available; many of them were either academic prototypes or proprietary languages of certain large companies or institutions.
Two well established and broadly used real-time languages are mentioned here, ADA and PEARL.

ADA is probably the most used language for realtime applications. It has a number of good properties including most of the ones mentioned above. One major disadvantage, however, is that it is very large and complex. It includes almost any feature of all other modern languages and is thus hard to learn and use, and it is difficult to produce efficient code.

PEARL [4] has been designed and standardised by a group of German scientists in early 70's and has also been re-defined in late 90's (PEARLSO). It also fulfills most of the above requirements; it is well understandable, and much simpler and closer to the control engineer than ADA. Among its drawbacks it is to be mentioned that it is not broadly used outside of Germany and Europe and does not have much support by other commercial program development tools.

In last years, object orientation is coming also into the real-time programming domain. The classical programming languages are being adapted to this paradigm, and new ones are emerging. The one to be mentioned in this context is Real-Time Java. Although the common Java is originating from the process control domain, there still are some obstacles to its consistent applicability, the most serious being the temporal impact of the garbage collection.

div.head: B. Industrial controller programmang
div.p: Vendors of programmable logic controllers usually provide their own programming tools. Most of their properties have been included in the IEC1131 standard [7] with the goal to uniform the program design.

They may be grouped into the five categories: instruction list: a low level assembly-like language; ladder diagram: logic functions expressed in a form of relay-logic; function block diagram: standard-and commonused routines are represented by blocks which are then "wired" together; structured text: structured high-level-like language; sequential function chart: graphic representation of the program structure on the task level, including parallel and alternative execution, etc.

While the first two are merely meant for compatibility with some older systems, the latter three represent powerful1 tools for application design. They could even be usable for programming of generic control computers: standard procedures are programmed, analysed and verified, and put into ROMs. The application programmer merely needs to "wire" them together into the specific application. This way, the complexity of the design could be greatly reduced and the verification of the programs composed of standard program blocks would be extremely simple.

div.head: C. Worst-case execution tame analysis
div.p: For schedulability analysis, execution times of programs must be known a priori. This is only possible if the language provides for predictability of program's temporal behaviour. Unfortunately, no programming language guarrantees that; it is necessary to introduce certain restrictions to its features:

GOTOs are not allowed: their use can result in unstructured code which is difficult to manage. Instead, EXIT and LOOP statements are introduced. The former is used for preliminary exit from innermost structures, and the latter is used in the REPEAT construct for immediate initiation of the next iteration of the loop. As a consequence, labels, except for procedure and task declarations, are obsolete and therefore renounced.

Each loop block must tightly bounded: lower and upper counts of iterations must, be present and defined with compile-time-constant expressions, so that the longest execution time of a loop can be estimated. The "while" or "repeat" conditions should be replaced by explicit IF-EXIT statements within loops.

Pointers and recursion are not allowed: their use can result in severe memory-management problems. They can produce temporally non-deterministic actions, and cannot be considered in the a priori timing analysis.

Each synchronisation construct must be temporally bounded: synchronisation constructs (for example critical regions or semaphores) may take arbitrarily long times for their execution. This must be bounded in real-time systems. Each such command must be temporally guarded, and an explicitly defined action must be given if a time-out occurs.
Explicitly asserted execution times: In some cases, estimation may yield a very pessimistic execution time.

To resolve this problem, additional execution information must be given by the programmer. This can be done by adding new constructs (pragmas) into the program code, as proposed in [lo], [ll]. However, this method requires complex analysis, and is not feasible in all situations. To overcome this problem, the explicit execution time of a part of the code can be asserted by the system developer, overriding the estimated results with the asserted ones. However, for safety reasons, the block must be guarded by time-out control, and a time-out action must be present.

Task scheduler support: The scheduling algorithm in the OS kernel processor relies on the residual execution time of tasks. This time is computed from the maximum execution time of a task minus the accumulated running time. However, the actual execution time is expected to be shorter than the estimated one. To achieve a more reliable and realistic estimation of the residual time, it can be updated explicitly, whenever possible, by asserting the information about the residual execution time which is more gradually more precise as the task approaches its end.
To estimate the execution times of programs written in the high-level programming language, the following three steps are necessary:
In the first step, the HLL source code is parsed and analysed for the constructs like straight line code blocks, alternatives, condition evaluations, loops, etc.
In the second step, the duration of each straight line portion of assembly language (or machine) code is calculated. In further analysis, the straight line blocks are not observed any more.

Finally, in the third step, the nested structures in the compiled source code are searched recursively until the innermost one is located. This is then reduced by its worst-case execution time: alternatives are reduced to the execution time of the longest one; execution times of the loop bodies are multiplied by the maximal number of iterations; subroutine calls are reduced by their duration. Then, the same procedure is performed on the next enclosing nested structure. Finally, the recursive application up to the outermost structures yields the execution time of the program.

div.head: VI. S A F E T Y CRITICAL APPLICATIONS
div.p: It seems to be easier to assure dependable hardware architectures than dependable software. The reason for that is that verification methodologies and techniques for hardware design has been well established since quite a long time now. Hardware can be safety licensed for critical applications by licensing authorities (like TUV in Germany) using well established procedures.

Software itself is much more complex, taking in account the whole life cycle, from specifications, design, coding and compilation into the machine code which is actually the final result. There is a number of hazards to its integrity, from the common faults and errors in specifications and in all levels of the design, to the implementation problems like arithmetic precision (consider Arianne 5 disaster), to mention just some of them.

Licensing of the software based systems is extremely difficult. Although a lot of high quality and very sophisticated research has been done in the area of formal specification and verification of programs, the techniques are generally acceptable only in relatively simple cases. Also, they are not formally accepted by licensing authorities, since they themselves rely on complex computer tools which are inherently unsafe.

The only officially recognised method by German licensing authorities is diverse back-translation [8]. It consists of re-gaining a requirement specifications from the software under test by several, independently working licensors or groups. To eliminate possible effects of error-prone compilers. it must be done on the machine code read out of the target system. It is obvious that this method is only feasible for very limited applications like, e.g. safe shut-down backup systems. It is not usable for most industrial applications.

For that reasons, in extremely critical applications and systems, like safety backup systems in nuclear power plants or avionics, where safety is crucial and the formal license is necessary, usually only hardware based or trivially simple programmed systems can be licensed for the time being. However, due to economic reasons, it is necessary to provide such methods and technologies that program based systems of reasonable complexity will also be licensably safe. In this sense, some alternative control systems have been elaborated [5] which can be proven correct rigorously with reasonable effort even in systems with realistic complexity.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: To achieve the properties which were found necessary in the generic real-time systems research, it will be necessary to re-think the methods and techniques common in all areas of embedded control systems design. The price to be paid for better consistency and, consequently, better safety, usability, availability, etc., is worse processor utilisation. This is tolerable, considering the state-of-the-art in solid-state technology, and availability and prices of hardware components.
Even in extremely safety-critical systems it will be for economical reasons necessary to replace relay logic and hardware based systems with programmed ones.
In their development, however, it will be necessary to follow the generally known, but usually neglected, principles of the hard real-time systems design.

Last, but not least, guideline in the embedded control design must be simplicity: considering the state-of-theart in all areas of the design, and especially in verification, this is the only way to guarantee consistency of the functional and temporal behaviour of embedded control systems.
